```{python}
#| echo: false
import os, sys
sys.path.insert(0, os.environ.get("QUARTO_PROJECT_DIR", "../.."))
from _lib.plots import load, bars, line, ROLE, PALETTE

m2, m2d = load("04-m2-fp32-strict.json"), load("04-m2-fp32-defer.json")
m1 = load("04-m1-loop.json")["timing"]
e1 = load("05-e1-grid-fp32.json")["timing"]
e1_cfg = sum(v["configs"] for v in e1.values())
e1_rows = sum(v["rows"] for v in e1.values())
e1_s = sum(v["generate_s"] for v in e1.values())
loop_cps, e1_cps = m1["configs"] / m1["generate_s"], e1_cfg / e1_s
loop_rps, e1_rps = m1["rows"] / m1["generate_s"], e1_rows / e1_s

bs, bd = load("06-bench-strict.json"), load("06-bench-defer.json")
B, C = bs["B_batched_strict"], bd["C_batched_defer"]
n_conf = [r["configs"] for r in B]
a_cps = (bs["A_loop"]["configs_per_s"] + bd["A_loop"]["configs_per_s"]) / 2
per_batch = bs["batch_rows"] // bs["prompts"]
peakB = max(B, key=lambda r: r["configs_per_s"])
```

## The speed table

Same workload for every mode: M2, 11 settings × 24 prompts = 264 rows, 60 new tokens,
greedy, fp32, one TPU v5e chip, timed after a warm-up call with a sync on both ends.

| Mode | What runs | Time (264 rows) | Speed-up vs A | Same output as A? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | One setting at a time (loop) | `{python} f"{m2['loop_s']:.1f}"` s | 1× | – |
| B | Batched, eager Strict | `{python} f"{m2['batched_s']:.1f}"` s | `{python} f"{m2['speedup']:.1f}"`× | 264/264 |
| C | Batched, DeferAndFuse | `{python} f"{m2d['batched_s']:.1f}"` s | `{python} f"{m2d['speedup']:.1f}"`× | 264/264 |

Each batched mode is compared with a loop run in the same eager mode (Strict loop
`{python} f"{m2['loop_s']:.1f}"` s, DeferAndFuse loop `{python} f"{m2d['loop_s']:.1f}"` s).

```{python}
#| label: fig-speed
#| fig-cap: "Time to generate the 264 rows of M2 on a TPU v5e-1 (fp32)."
fig, ax = bars(["A loop", "B Strict", "C DeferAndFuse"],
               [m2["loop_s"], m2["batched_s"], m2d["batched_s"]],
               colors=[ROLE["control"], ROLE["steered"], PALETTE["teal"]], fmt="{:.1f} s",
               ylabel="seconds", source="data/04-m2-fp32-*.json")
```

**Batching is the win; fusion isn't (here).** Going from A to B is 4.4×. Going from B to C
changes almost nothing. That makes sense for this workload: a steering hook is a handful of
elementwise ops per block, small next to the matmuls of a 0.6B model, so fusing them saves
little, and decoding is limited by how many rows share each weight read, which is exactly
what batching changes.

## At sweep scale

M2 is small. The E1 sweep in [part 5](../05-results-maps/index.qmd) is the realistic case:
`{python} e1_cfg` settings, `{python} f"{e1_rows:,}"` rows, batch 256.

| | prompts per setting | settings / s |
|---|---|---|
| Loop (M1) | 24 | `{python} f"{loop_cps:.2f}"` |
| Loop (bench A, below) | `{python} bs["prompts"]` | `{python} f"{a_cps:.2f}"` |
| Batched sweep (E1) | 12 | `{python} f"{e1_cps:.2f}"` |

The loop's speed barely depends on how many prompts each setting has
(`{python} f"{loop_cps:.2f}"` settings/s at 24 prompts, `{python} f"{a_cps:.2f}"` at 12): one
small batch costs about the same either way. So the fair comparison is the bench below,
which runs loop and batched with 12 prompts per setting: about
**`{python} f"{peakB['speedup_vs_loop']:.0f}"`×** like for like. The 672-setting map takes a few
minutes of generation instead of nearly an hour.

## How many settings fill the chip?

The bench below runs E1-style pushes (12 prompts per setting, 60 new tokens) with
more and more settings at once. One batch holds `{python} bs["batch_rows"]` rows, so
`{python} per_batch` settings fill it; bigger sweeps run as several full batches.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scaling
#| fig-cap: "Settings per second vs how many settings are swept at once (12 prompts each, batch of up to 256 rows). The dashed line is the one-at-a-time loop."
fig, ax = line(n_conf, {"B Strict": [r["configs_per_s"] for r in B],
                        "C DeferAndFuse": [r["configs_per_s"] for r in C]},
               hlines={"A loop": a_cps},
               colors={"B Strict": ROLE["steered"], "C DeferAndFuse": PALETTE["teal"], "A loop": ROLE["control"]},
               xlabel="settings in the sweep", ylabel="settings / s",
               source="data/06-bench-*.json")
ax.set_xscale("log", base=2); ax.set_xticks(n_conf, [str(n) for n in n_conf]); ax.set_ylim(0, None);
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print("| settings | rows | B Strict (settings/s) | C DeferAndFuse | speed-up of B vs loop |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|")
for b, c in zip(B, C):
    print(f"| {b['configs']} | {b['rows']:,} | {b['configs_per_s']:.2f} | {c['configs_per_s']:.2f} | {b['speedup_vs_loop']:.1f}× |")
```

Throughput climbs while the batch fills up, then flattens at about `{python} f"{peakB['configs_per_s']:.1f}"` settings/s, roughly `{python} f"{peakB['speedup_vs_loop']:.0f}"`× the loop (`{python} f"{a_cps:.2f}"` settings/s). With 8 settings the batch is only 96 rows and the chip
sits partly idle. From about 64 settings (three full batches) on, nearly every batch is full
and adding settings just adds batches. B and C stay within noise of each other at every size, which matches the
speed table above.

So for this model the rule is simple: sweep enough settings to fill whole batches of 256
rows, and beyond that the cost is linear. (In bf16, batches must stay at 128 rows or
fewer for now; see [part 4](../04-one-row-per-experiment/index.qmd).)

## Next: torch.compile and XProf

Two things were not measured in this sprint. The first is a fourth mode,
`torch.compile(model, backend="tpu")`: its compile time, steady-state speed, and whether
its outputs match the loop. The second is XProf traces of Strict and DeferAndFuse side by
side, which would show where each decode step spends its time and what DeferAndFuse
actually fuses. Both are the natural next step. The numbers above say batching is where
most of the win is; whether compiling adds anything on top of the ~15× is still open.
